questions.prompt: How would you normalise a NumPy array of values to the range 0 to 1 and what can go wrong?
questions.ideal_answer: Subtract the minimum and divide by the range, max minus min. If all values are equal the range is zero and you divide by zero, and outliers squeeze the rest of the data, so check for both and compute the statistics on training data only.
follow_ups: How is standardisation different?

questions.prompt: How would you design Python classes for a text classification pipeline with a preprocessor and a model?
questions.ideal_answer: Create a Preprocessor class with fit and transform and a Model class with train and predict, then a Pipeline class that connects them so the same preprocessing is used in training and prediction. Keep each part testable.
follow_ups: Why does scikit-learn use this pattern?

questions.prompt: Your script compares each of 100,000 items against a list of 50,000 banned words. How do you make it fast?
questions.ideal_answer: Put the banned words in a set so each check is O(1) on average instead of scanning the list, and normalise case once. This changes O(n times m) into O(n plus m).
follow_ups: What if you need prefix matches?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between classification and regression, and what is logistic regression used for?
questions.ideal_answer: Classification predicts a category and regression predicts a number. Logistic regression predicts the probability of a class using a sigmoid on a linear combination of features, and it is a strong simple baseline for binary problems.
follow_ups: How do you choose the decision threshold?

questions.prompt: What do L1 and L2 regularisation do and when would you use each?
questions.ideal_answer: Both add a penalty on large weights to reduce overfitting. L2 shrinks weights smoothly, while L1 can push some to exactly zero and so selects features. Use L1 for sparse feature selection and L2 as the general default.
follow_ups: How is the strength of the penalty chosen?

questions.prompt: How does k-means clustering work and how do you choose k?
questions.ideal_answer: K-means picks k centres, assigns each point to the nearest centre, moves each centre to the mean of its points and repeats until stable. Choose k with the elbow method, silhouette score or domain knowledge, and scale the features first.
follow_ups: What are its weaknesses?

questions.prompt: Why must you split time-series data by time instead of randomly, and how do you cross-validate it?
questions.ideal_answer: A random split lets the model train on the future and test on the past, which leaks information. Use a time-ordered split and forward-chaining validation where each fold trains on earlier data and tests on later data.
key_points: Train on past, test on future
follow_ups: What else can leak in time-series features?

questions.prompt: How do you tune hyperparameters without overfitting the validation set?
questions.ideal_answer: Use cross-validation with grid, random or Bayesian search, keep a final test set untouched until the end and prefer simpler settings when scores are similar. Record the search so it can be reproduced.
follow_ups: Why is random search often better than grid search?

questions.prompt: What are the signs of vanishing gradients and overfitting in a neural network and how do you address them?
questions.ideal_answer: Vanishing gradients show up as early layers barely learning, addressed with ReLU-type activations, good initialisation, normalisation and residual connections. Overfitting shows as a growing gap between training and validation loss, addressed with dropout, data augmentation, regularisation and early stopping.
follow_ups: What does batch normalisation do?

questions.prompt: Why do transformers use positional encoding and what limits their input length?
questions.ideal_answer: Attention treats tokens as a set, so positional encoding gives the model word order. Attention cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which limits context size and memory, leading to techniques such as sparse or efficient attention.
follow_ups: What is a context window?

questions.prompt: What text preprocessing steps are common in NLP and when can they hurt?
questions.ideal_answer: Lowercasing, removing punctuation and stop words, tokenising and stemming or lemmatising are common. They can hurt when they remove meaning, such as negation words or case in names, and modern transformer models usually need little of this.
follow_ups: Why keep the word 'not' in sentiment analysis?

questions.prompt: Compare TF-IDF with word embeddings for representing text.
questions.ideal_answer: TF-IDF counts words weighted by how rare they are, is sparse and ignores meaning, while embeddings are dense vectors that place similar meanings close together. TF-IDF is a fast strong baseline and embeddings capture semantics.
follow_ups: When would TF-IDF still win?

questions.prompt: How would you evaluate a text summarisation system when there is no single correct summary?
questions.ideal_answer: Combine automatic overlap metrics such as ROUGE with embedding-based scores and, more importantly, human or carefully designed model-based judgements for faithfulness, coverage and clarity. Check against hallucinated facts.
follow_ups: Why can ROUGE be misleading?

questions.prompt: What are few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting and when do they help?
questions.ideal_answer: Few-shot prompting gives examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern, and chain-of-thought asks it to reason step by step, which can improve multi-step problems. They cost more tokens and reasoning text should still be verified.
follow_ups: How would you test that examples help?

questions.prompt: What is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA, and why is it used?
questions.ideal_answer: It trains a small number of added parameters while keeping the base model frozen, which needs far less memory and time than full fine-tuning and allows several lightweight adapters. Quality depends on data and the task.
follow_ups: When is full fine-tuning justified?

questions.prompt: Why combine keyword search with vector search in a RAG system?
questions.ideal_answer: Vector search finds meaning but can miss exact terms such as names, codes or numbers, while keyword search finds exact matches. A hybrid search with re-ranking gets the best of both.
follow_ups: What does a re-ranker do?

questions.prompt: What controls would you put on an AI agent that can call tools such as email or a database?
questions.ideal_answer: Give it the least privilege, require human approval for risky actions, validate tool inputs, limit the number of steps and cost, log every action and defend against prompt injection from retrieved content.
follow_ups: How would you test the agent's safety?

questions.prompt: You get a labelled dataset where some labels are clearly wrong. How do you detect and handle this?
questions.ideal_answer: Inspect samples, look at examples the model predicts confidently differently from the label, compare annotators for agreement, correct or remove noisy labels and use robust methods. Fix the labelling process.
follow_ups: How much noise can a model tolerate?

questions.prompt: Write the idea of a query to find users who made a purchase in the last 7 days but none in the 30 days before that.
questions.ideal_answer: Select users with orders in the last 7 days and exclude those with any order between day 37 and day 7 ago using NOT EXISTS or a left join with IS NULL.
follow_ups: How would you turn this into a retention metric?

questions.prompt: How do you detect that a deployed model has degraded?
questions.ideal_answer: Monitor input feature distributions for drift, prediction distributions, latency and errors, and compare predictions to real outcomes when labels arrive. Alert on thresholds and keep a retraining plan.
follow_ups: What if labels arrive weeks later?

questions.prompt: Scenario: your sentiment model works well on your test data but fails on customer reviews written in mixed English and Urdu. What do you do?
questions.ideal_answer: Collect and label samples of the real data, measure the failure by language, consider a multilingual model or transliteration handling, add the data to training and keep a test set that reflects real use.
follow_ups: How would you get labels cheaply?

questions.prompt: Scenario: design a system that flags fraudulent transactions in real time with very few labelled fraud cases.
questions.ideal_answer: Combine rules, an anomaly or supervised model trained with careful handling of imbalance, score transactions in milliseconds, route borderline cases to human review and use their decisions as new labels. Monitor false positives.
follow_ups: How do you handle changing fraud patterns?

questions.prompt: Scenario: a non-technical manager asks whether your model is good enough to launch. How do you answer?
questions.ideal_answer: Explain performance in terms of business impact, compare it with the current process or a baseline, state its limits and risks and propose a small pilot with monitoring before full launch.
follow_ups: What would make you say not yet?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a library such as scikit-learn and a deep learning framework such as PyTorch, and when do you use each?
questions.ideal_answer: Scikit-learn offers classic machine learning algorithms and tools for tabular data with a simple fit and predict interface. PyTorch builds and trains neural networks with automatic differentiation and GPU support. Use scikit-learn for tabular baselines and PyTorch for deep models on images, text or audio.
follow_ups: Why start with a simple baseline?

questions.prompt: Describe an AI or ML project in detail: the data, the approach, the metric and one thing that did not work.
questions.ideal_answer: A strong answer is specific about the dataset and your steps, justifies the metric, explains an honest failure and what you learned, and separates your work from borrowed code.
follow_ups: What would you try next?
